title: Extra: thermometers and imperial units
summary: Read a thermometer in °C, then meet inches, feet, pounds and pints and their metric equivalents.
guide: We measure {{term:temperature}} with a thermometer, in degrees Celsius (°C). Water freezes at 0 °C.
Not every mark on a thermometer has a number. First work out what each small mark is worth, then count on.
Temperatures below zero are negative: −6 °C means 6 degrees below zero. The lower it is, the colder it is.
Imperial units are older units still used in the UK. 1 foot = 12 inches, 1 yard = 3 feet, 1 mile = 1760 yards.
Rough metric equivalents: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds (lb), 1 pint ≈ 570 ml, 5 miles ≈ 8 km.

read-thermometer.title: How warm is it today?
read-thermometer.prompt: Fatima looks at the thermometer in the yard. First: what is each small mark worth? Now write the temperature.
read-thermometer.hint: Between 20 and 30 there are 4 small marks and 5 spaces. 10 ÷ 5 = 2, so each mark is 2 °C. Count on in twos from 20.
read-thermometer.why: How did you know each small mark is 2 degrees, not 1?
read-thermometer.model: From 20 to 30 is 10 degrees, split into 5 spaces. 10 ÷ 5 = 2, so each space is 2 degrees. Three marks above 20 is 20 + 6 = 26.

feedback.mark-size: You counted each small mark as 1 degree. Count the spaces between 20 and 30: each mark is 2 degrees.
feedback.rounded: The level is not exactly on a number. Count the small marks too.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. Count the marks from 20 again.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. Count the marks from 20 again.
feedback.empty: Write the temperature as a number.

below-zero.title: Below zero
below-zero.prompt: On a winter night it is −6 °C. Set the thermometer to −6 °C.
below-zero.hint: First go down to 0. Then go 6 degrees further down. Each mark is 2 degrees, so that is 3 marks.
below-zero.model: −2 °C is warmer. On the thermometer −2 is higher than −6, and higher is warmer. −6 °C is 6 degrees colder than freezing.

feedback.above-zero: That is 6 °C, above zero. −6 °C is below zero.
feedback.counted-up: That is −4 °C. Go 3 marks down from 0.
feedback.too-big: That is still warmer than −6 °C. Go down further.
feedback.too-small: You went too far down. Go up a little.

inches-to-cm.title: A pencil in inches
inches-to-cm.prompt: This ruler is in inches. First read the pencil's length in inches. Then, using 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm, about how many centimetres is it?
inches-to-cm.hint: The pencil reaches the 6. Each inch is about 2.5 cm, so work out 6 × 2.5.
inches-to-cm.why: Why is the number of centimetres bigger than the number of inches?
inches-to-cm.model: A centimetre is smaller than an inch: about 2.5 cm fit into 1 inch. A smaller unit fits more times into the same pencil, so the number is bigger.

feedback.inches: 6 is the length in inches. Now change it to centimetres: each inch is about 2.5 cm.
feedback.added: You added 2.5. Each inch is 2.5 cm, so multiply: 6 × 2.5.
feedback.divided: You divided. Centimetres are smaller, so there are more of them: multiply.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. Work out 6 × 2.5.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. Work out 6 × 2.5.

feet-and-inches.title: Feet and inches
feet-and-inches.prompt: Hassan is 4 feet 6 inches tall. How many inches is that altogether? The strip shows the imperial units for length.
feet-and-inches.hint: Look at the strip: 1 foot = 12 inches. So 4 feet = 4 × 12 inches. Then add the 6.
feet-and-inches.why: Why is 4 feet 6 inches not 46 inches?
feet-and-inches.model: Feet and inches are not tens and ones. A foot is 12 inches, not 10. So 4 feet is 48 inches, and 48 + 6 = 54.

feedback.base-ten: Feet and inches do not work like tens and ones: 1 foot is 12 inches. Work out 4 × 12 first.
feedback.wrong-factor: Check the strip: 1 foot is 12 inches, and there are 4 feet. Then add the 6 inches.

kg-to-pounds.title: Kilograms and pounds
kg-to-pounds.prompt: Read the scale in kilograms. Then, using 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds, about how many pounds (lb) does the bag weigh?
kg-to-pounds.hint: The needle is on 2 kg. Each kilogram is about 2.2 lb, so work out 2 × 2.2.
kg-to-pounds.why: Is a pound heavier or lighter than a kilogram? How do you know?
kg-to-pounds.model: Lighter. More than 2 pounds make one kilogram, so one pound must be less than half a kilogram.

feedback.wrote-kg: 2 is the mass in kilograms. Now change it to pounds: each kilogram is about 2.2 lb.
feedback.divided: You divided. A pound is lighter than a kilogram, so there are more pounds: multiply.
feedback.too-big: Your number is too big. Work out 2 × 2.2.
feedback.too-small: Your number is too small. Work out 2 × 2.2.

pint-of-milk.title: A pint of milk
pint-of-milk.prompt: A pint is about 570 ml. Pour one pint of milk into the jug, as close as the marks allow.
pint-of-milk.hint: There is a mark every 50 ml. 570 is between 550 and 600. Which mark is closer?
pint-of-milk.success: Well done! 550 ml is the closest mark to one pint (568 ml).
pint-of-milk.why: Is a pint more or less than half a litre? How do you know?
pint-of-milk.model: More. Half a litre is 500 ml and a pint is about 570 ml. So a pint is a bit more than half a litre.

feedback.half-litre: That is half a litre, 500 ml. A pint is a bit more.
feedback.litre: That is a whole litre. A pint is only a bit more than half a litre.
feedback.too-big: That is too much milk. Pour some out.
feedback.too-small: Not enough milk yet. Pour in more.
